title: Acute Compartment Syndrome: Pain Out of Proportion Is the Warning
bottomLine: Acute compartment syndrome is limb-threatening pressure within a closed muscle compartment. Severe escalating pain out of proportion to injury, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia or new motor deficit require immediate orthopedic escalation. Pulses may remain present until late.
recognize: Disproportionate pain despite analgesia
Pain with passive stretch
Tense swollen compartment, paresthesia, weakness
Pulselessness and pallor are late findings
assess: Frequent neurovascular checks: pain, sensation, movement, color, temperature, cap refill and pulses
Inspect casts/splints/dressings for constriction
Compare with the unaffected extremity and trend changes
actions: Notify the surgical/orthopedic team immediately
Remove or loosen external constriction only according to emergency protocol/order
Keep the extremity near heart level rather than high elevation when compartment syndrome is suspected
Prepare for emergent fasciotomy
diagnostics: Diagnosis is clinical in a high-risk presentation; compartment-pressure measurement can support uncertain cases
Do not delay urgent surgical evaluation while waiting for pulse loss
medicationSafety: Analgesia is appropriate but should not mask repeated reassessment
Regional anesthesia or heavy sedation can make symptom monitoring harder and requires an appropriate monitoring plan
teaching: After fracture/casting, report increasing pain, numbness, weakness, tightness, coolness or inability to move digits immediately
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs neurovascular surveillance and reports deterioration immediately. Splitting casts, pressure measurement and fasciotomy decisions are performed by authorized clinicians.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient because distal pulses are present despite severe escalating pain and paresthesia.
oneLinePearl: Compartment syndrome hurts before the pulse disappears.
sourceBasis: 2025 AAOS Acute Compartment Syndrome Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Fractures and Casts: Alignment, Perfusion, Pressure, and Embolism
bottomLine: After fracture reduction or casting, the nursing priority is repeated neurovascular assessment and early recognition of compartment syndrome, skin pressure, infection, DVT or fat embolism. A cast that becomes painfully tight with neurologic change is not simply expected swelling.
recognize: Expected fracture pain/swelling should improve with treatment and time
New numbness, weakness, coolness, color change or disproportionate pain suggests neurovascular compromise
Fat embolism syndrome after major long-bone trauma can cause respiratory distress, neurologic change and petechial rash
assess: Pain, pulses, cap refill, color, temperature, sensation and movement distal to injury
Cast edges/skin/odor/drainage and swelling
Respiratory and neuro status after major long-bone trauma
actions: Elevate early uncomplicated swelling as ordered while continuing neurovascular checks
Protect a wet cast with palms rather than fingertips and allow proper drying
Escalate neurovascular compromise immediately
Use VTE prevention and mobility plan as ordered
diagnostics: New respiratory/neuro deterioration after long-bone trauma needs emergency evaluation rather than routine cast care
medicationSafety: Opioids require sedation/respiratory monitoring
Anticoagulant prophylaxis increases bleeding risk but should not be stopped independently
teaching: Keep cast dry unless specifically designed otherwise, never insert objects inside, and report increasing pain, numbness, foul drainage or breathing change
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs routine cast and neurovascular care within competency and escalates abnormalities. Reduction/alignment decisions are provider-directed.
examTrap: Using a hair dryer on hot setting or inserting an object under the cast to scratch itching.
oneLinePearl: Fracture follow-up: pain, perfusion, pressure, lungs.
sourceBasis: AAOS fracture and trauma care principles

title: Hip Fracture in Older Adults: Pain Control Plus Early Recovery
bottomLine: Hip fracture in an older adult threatens mobility, cognition, respiratory function, skin and survival. Provide multimodal pain control, delirium and VTE prevention, pulmonary hygiene, nutrition, pressure protection and early mobilization after repair according to the surgical plan.
recognize: Pain, inability to bear weight, shortened/external-rotated leg may occur but are not required
Older adults may present after a low-energy fall
Delirium and deconditioning can develop rapidly during hospitalization
assess: Pain, neurovascular status, cognition/baseline, respiratory function, skin, hydration and bowel/bladder
Assess cause of fall and anticoagulant use
Post-op monitor wound, hemoglobin, mobility and complications
actions: Handle injured limb carefully and provide ordered analgesia
Prepare for timely surgical repair when planned
Mobilize early with PT/OT and prescribed weight-bearing status
Prevent delirium, VTE, constipation, pressure injury and atelectasis
diagnostics: X-ray is first-line; occult fracture can require MRI/advanced imaging when suspicion persists
medicationSafety: Opioids can worsen delirium/constipation but uncontrolled pain also worsens delirium
Anticoagulant management around surgery is individualized
teaching: Fall prevention, osteoporosis evaluation/treatment, home safety, mobility device use and rehabilitation adherence
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports pre/post-op care, pain and mobility assessment, and complication prevention. Weight-bearing and surgical plans are directed by the orthopedic team.
examTrap: Keeping the postoperative patient on bedrest for several days because movement seems risky.
oneLinePearl: Hip fracture recovery starts early: pain controlled, patient moving, delirium prevented.
sourceBasis: AAOS Management of Hip Fractures in Older Adults Guideline

title: Joint Replacement: DVT, Infection, Dislocation, Mobility
bottomLine: After hip or knee arthroplasty, priorities are pain control, early safe mobility, VTE prevention, wound/infection surveillance and operation-specific precautions. Sudden severe pain, deformity, shortening/rotation, new neurovascular change, fever with drainage, or PE symptoms require rapid evaluation.
recognize: Expected postoperative pain/swelling should trend down
DVT/PE and infection are major complications
Dislocation precautions depend on surgical approach and surgeon instructions—not one universal list
assess: Pain, wound, temperature, distal neurovascular status, mobility
DVT/PE symptoms and anticoagulant bleeding
Ability to transfer safely with prescribed assistive device
actions: Mobilize with PT/OT and prescribed weight-bearing status
Give VTE prophylaxis and pain regimen as ordered
Use operation-specific hip precautions only when prescribed
Escalate suspected dislocation or infection
diagnostics: Imaging evaluates suspected dislocation or hardware complication
CBC/inflammatory tests/cultures are selected when infection suspected
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants increase bleeding risk
Opioids require bowel and respiratory/sedation monitoring
Antibiotics are prophylaxis/treatment-specific rather than continued indefinitely
teaching: Follow individualized activity and hip-position precautions, wound care and VTE prevention; use dental/procedure antibiotic prophylaxis only if specifically recommended
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports routine post-op assessment and mobility within the plan. Do not invent universal movement restrictions for all hip approaches.
examTrap: Teaching every hip replacement patient the same classic posterior-approach restrictions regardless of actual surgical approach.
oneLinePearl: Joint replacement: move safely, prevent clot, watch wound, know the actual approach precautions.

title: Traction: Maintain the Line of Pull
bottomLine: Traction works only when the prescribed line of pull and countertraction are maintained. Weights should hang freely unless the treatment plan specifically says otherwise; keep ropes unobstructed, body aligned and skin/pin/neurovascular status monitored.
recognize: Misalignment, weights resting on floor/bed, tangled ropes or displaced pulleys reduce effectiveness
Skin traction can cause pressure injury
Skeletal traction pin sites can become infected
assess: Body alignment and line of pull
Weights/ropes/pulleys
Neurovascular status, skin, pain and pin sites
Mobility, elimination and pressure-risk complications
actions: Maintain prescribed weights and free-hanging system
Reposition using the authorized method without disrupting traction
Perform pin/skin care according to protocol
Prevent immobility complications
diagnostics: Imaging may monitor fracture alignment; bedside nursing assessment focuses on traction mechanics and patient complications
medicationSafety: Analgesia should support safe care without oversedation
teaching: Do not alter weights or remove traction without staff instruction
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN may manage routine traction care according to competency but should not independently change prescribed weights or traction configuration.
examTrap: Removing traction weights temporarily for repositioning because it seems more comfortable.
oneLinePearl: Traction must stay continuous, aligned and freely weighted.

title: Pressure Injury Prevention: Pressure, Moisture, Friction, Nutrition, Mobility
bottomLine: Pressure injuries are prevented with individualized risk assessment, regular skin inspection, pressure redistribution, repositioning/mobility, moisture management and nutrition support. Do not massage reddened bony prominences or use donut-style devices that concentrate pressure.
recognize: Nonblanchable redness or persistent discoloration over pressure areas is an early warning
Darkly pigmented skin may show temperature, firmness or color changes that are subtler than visible redness
Medical devices create pressure risk at ears, nose, tubing and immobilization points
assess: Head-to-toe skin including under devices
Mobility, moisture/incontinence, nutrition/hydration, perfusion and sensation
Use a validated risk tool as one part of clinical assessment
actions: Reposition based on patient and support surface rather than rigid clock-only care
Offload heels and high-risk areas
Use moisture barriers and appropriate support surfaces
Optimize nutrition and mobility
diagnostics: Pressure-injury staging is based on tissue presentation; do not reverse-stage a healing wound
medicationSafety: Analgesia may be needed for wound care; topical agents should match wound indication rather than be applied routinely
teaching: Frequent position change, skin checks, moisture control and nutrition are prevention tools for patients/caregivers
scopeAndDelegation: Assistive personnel can reposition and provide skin hygiene, but the nurse must assess skin changes and update the care plan/escalate abnormalities.
examTrap: Massaging a nonblanchable red heel to increase circulation.
oneLinePearl: Prevent pressure injury by offloading pressure and controlling moisture while preserving movement and nutrition.
sourceBasis: AHRQ Skin Under Pressure: Preventing Pressure Injury Toolkit

title: Major Burns: Airway, Burn Size, Perfusion, Temperature
bottomLine: Major burn priorities are airway/inhalation injury, burn depth and total body surface area, circulation and fluid resuscitation, temperature control, pain, wound protection and burn-center referral. Facial burns, soot, hoarseness or enclosed-space fire exposure can precede rapid airway edema.
recognize: Inhalation injury clues: facial burns, singed hair, soot, carbonaceous sputum, hoarseness, enclosed-space exposure
Circumferential burns can impair limb or chest perfusion/ventilation
Large burns cause capillary leak and hypovolemic burn shock
assess: Airway/voice/breathing, SpO2 plus carbon-monoxide exposure context
Burn depth/TBSA and mechanism
Perfusion, urine output, temperature, pain and neurovascular status
actions: Stop burning process and remove constricting items
Provide high-concentration oxygen for suspected smoke/carbon monoxide exposure according to emergency protocol
Start ordered burn fluid resuscitation and titrate to clinical endpoints
Cover burns with clean dry material initially and prevent hypothermia
Arrange burn-center consultation/referral when criteria met
diagnostics: Carboxyhemoglobin requires co-oximetry; conventional pulse oximetry can look falsely reassuring in carbon monoxide exposure
Electrolytes, blood gas/lactate and imaging are mechanism/severity driven
medicationSafety: IV opioids are often needed in major burns and require respiratory monitoring
Avoid routine prophylactic systemic antibiotics for uncomplicated clean burns without infection indication
teaching: Burn wound care, infection signs, scar/rehab plan and smoke/fire prevention are individualized after stabilization
scopeAndDelegation: Major-burn resuscitation and escharotomy are specialty/team directed. PN/LVN priorities are rapid airway/perfusion recognition, ordered supportive care and escalation.
examTrap: Relying on a normal pulse-ox reading to exclude carbon monoxide poisoning after an enclosed-space fire.
oneLinePearl: Burn first look: airway, size/depth, perfusion, temperature.
sourceBasis: American Burn Association Clinical Practice and Burn Center Referral Guidelines

title: Dehiscence and Evisceration: Protect the Organs, Reduce Strain
bottomLine: If an abdominal incision opens with exposed organs, this is evisceration: call for immediate surgical help, keep the patient from straining, cover the organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings according to emergency policy, keep NPO, and prepare for return to surgery. Never push organs back into the abdomen.
recognize: Dehiscence: separation of wound layers
Evisceration: abdominal contents protrude through the wound
A sudden gush of serosanguineous drainage can precede wound separation
assess: Airway/hemodynamics, wound separation, bleeding, pain and signs of infection
Recent coughing/vomiting/straining and risk factors such as infection, malnutrition or obesity
actions: Stay with patient and call surgical/emergency support
Position to reduce abdominal tension as tolerated
Cover exposed tissue with sterile saline-moistened dressings
Keep NPO and prepare for operative repair
diagnostics: This is a clinical surgical emergency; imaging should not delay direct surgical evaluation when evisceration is obvious
medicationSafety: Provide ordered analgesia and antibiotics while maintaining assessment; do not apply unapproved topical agents directly to exposed organs
teaching: Splint incision during coughing, follow lifting restrictions and report sudden drainage/opening promptly
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN initiates emergency wound protection and escalation according to policy. Surgical closure is not a bedside nursing task.
examTrap: Attempting to gently push protruding bowel back through the incision.
oneLinePearl: Evisceration: cover moist, reduce strain, NPO, surgery now.
sourceBasis: CDC surgical-site and perioperative wound principles

title: Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection: Pain Out of Proportion Plus Toxicity
bottomLine: Rapidly progressive severe soft-tissue pain out of proportion to visible findings, swelling, systemic toxicity, bullae, skin discoloration, crepitus or anesthesia can signal necrotizing infection. Treat as a surgical and sepsis emergency: antibiotics and resuscitation matter, but source control cannot wait.
recognize: Severe disproportionate pain early
Rapid progression, edema beyond erythema, dusky skin/bullae
Crepitus may occur but is not required
Later numbness can reflect nerve destruction, not improvement
assess: Vitals/perfusion, pain trend, extent of swelling/color, mental status
Mark/track spread when helpful without delaying surgery
Assess diabetes, immune compromise, wound/trauma or recent surgery
actions: Activate sepsis and surgical emergency pathways
Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics and fluids as ordered
Prepare for urgent operative exploration/debridement
Use appropriate isolation/wound precautions
diagnostics: Labs/imaging can support diagnosis, but high clinical suspicion should not be delayed for imaging when surgical emergency is apparent
medicationSafety: Clindamycin or other toxin-suppressing therapy may be added for selected streptococcal/clostridial disease under protocol
Pain medication should not delay reassessment or source control
teaching: Seek urgent care for rapidly worsening wound pain, swelling, fever or discoloration
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN recognizes the red-flag pattern, starts ordered sepsis therapy and escalates. Surgical exploration/debridement is definitive team care.
examTrap: Waiting for obvious black necrosis before escalating severe rapidly progressive pain and systemic illness.
oneLinePearl: Nec fasc: disproportionate pain plus rapid toxicity means surgery fast.
sourceBasis: IDSA Skin and Soft Tissue Infection Guidance

title: Osteomyelitis: Bone Infection Needs Time and Source Control
bottomLine: Osteomyelitis can follow contiguous wounds, diabetic foot infection, surgery/hardware or bloodstream spread. Expect prolonged targeted antimicrobial therapy and possible debridement; monitor wound, pain, fever, inflammatory markers, renal/drug toxicity and line complications rather than assuming symptom improvement means the infection is cured.
recognize: Localized bone pain/tenderness, draining sinus or chronic wound
Fever may be absent in chronic disease
Diabetes/neuropathy and hardware increase risk
assess: Wound depth/drainage, pain, fever, limb perfusion and glucose control
Medication and IV-access effects
Trend cultures/inflammatory and renal tests as ordered
actions: Obtain ordered deep/tissue or blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible
Administer prolonged targeted antimicrobials exactly on schedule
Support wound offloading and surgical source control
Escalate sepsis or limb ischemia
diagnostics: MRI is useful for many suspected cases
Bone/tissue culture is more definitive than superficial swab for selecting therapy
medicationSafety: Long antibiotic courses create renal, hepatic, marrow and C. difficile risks
PICC/central access requires infection and thrombosis surveillance
teaching: Complete therapy, perform wound/foot care and offloading, manage diabetes/smoking and keep follow-up even after pain improves
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN supports wound and antimicrobial care and monitors complications. Debridement and antibiotic duration are specialist-directed.
examTrap: Using a superficial wound swab as though it proves the organism causing deep bone infection.
oneLinePearl: Bone infection is a long game: culture, antibiotics, source control, follow-up.

title: Osteoporosis: Prevent the Fracture Before the Fall Happens
bottomLine: Osteoporosis often has no symptoms until a fragility fracture. Prevention combines adequate calcium/vitamin D intake, weight-bearing/resistance activity, smoking/alcohol risk reduction, fall prevention and indicated pharmacologic therapy; a low-trauma hip or vertebral fracture is a major signal for secondary prevention.
recognize: Fragility fracture after low-energy fall
Height loss or vertebral compression fractures
Risks include age, low body weight, glucocorticoids, smoking, hypogonadism and selected diseases/medications
assess: Fall history, mobility, vision, medications, nutrition and fracture history
DXA and secondary-cause labs as ordered
Dental/renal/GI factors that affect medication choice
actions: Support exercise and fall-prevention plan
Administer antiresorptive/anabolic therapy as ordered
Ensure calcium/vitamin D plan is appropriate to diet and medical history
diagnostics: DXA measures bone mineral density; fracture risk combines BMD with clinical factors
Vertebral fractures may be clinically silent
medicationSafety: Oral bisphosphonates require specific administration to reduce esophageal injury
Denosumab discontinuation requires a transition plan because rebound vertebral fracture risk can occur
Long-term therapy monitoring is agent-specific
redFlags: New severe back pain with neuro symptoms
Atypical femur pain on long-term antiresorptive therapy
Jaw healing problems in high-risk treatment contexts
teaching: Correct oral bisphosphonate technique, fall prevention, exercise, smoking cessation and medication adherence
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN reinforces prevention and administration instructions and reports adverse effects. Drug selection and duration are prescriber-directed.
examTrap: Teaching a patient to take an oral bisphosphonate with breakfast and lie down afterward.
oneLinePearl: Osteoporosis is silent until fracture—prevention and post-fracture treatment matter.
sourceBasis: Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation clinical guidance

title: Surgical Wounds: Expected Inflammation vs Surgical-Site Infection
bottomLine: A healing incision may have mild localized tenderness and limited early inflammation, but increasing erythema, warmth, purulent/cloudy drainage, wound separation, fever, escalating pain or systemic illness suggests surgical-site infection or deeper complication. Use aseptic wound care and obtain ordered specimens correctly.
recognize: Worsening rather than improving pain/redness
Purulent or cloudy drainage and wound separation
Deep/organ-space infection may produce systemic illness with little superficial change
assess: Incision edges, drainage amount/color/odor, surrounding skin, pain, temperature
Systemic signs and glucose control
Devices/drains and postoperative timeline
actions: Perform hand hygiene and wound care using ordered aseptic technique
Notify the surgical team of concerning progression
Collect deep/appropriate specimens rather than contaminating superficial samples when ordered
Administer antibiotics and support source control as ordered
diagnostics: Cultures and imaging depend on infection depth and clinical severity
Do not routinely apply topical antimicrobials to closed surgical incisions solely to prevent infection unless specifically indicated
medicationSafety: Antibiotics should match the infection and source-control plan
Monitor analgesics and antibiotic adverse effects
teaching: Hand hygiene, wound instructions and early reporting of drainage, fever, opening or worsening pain
scopeAndDelegation: PN/LVN performs ordered wound care and identifies infection/dehiscence changes. Assistive personnel can help with hygiene but must not independently assess or stage surgical-wound complications.
examTrap: Applying antibiotic ointment routinely to every clean closed incision because it seems safer.
oneLinePearl: A surgical wound should trend better; worsening pain, drainage or separation needs review.
sourceBasis: CDC Surgical Site Infection Prevention Guideline
